concepts.title: Features of a Company
concepts.definition: A joint stock company is a body brought into existence by law, owned in fractions by shareholders and run day to day by a board they elect; it owns property, contracts and holds bank accounts in its own name.
concepts.key_idea: Members may join, exit, die or turn insolvent, yet the company lives on until the law itself winds it up.

solution_steps.explain: the company is incorporated under the Companies Act and thereby becomes a person distinct from the people who own it
shareholders own shares, their risk stops at unpaid money on those shares, and they govern through an elected board rather than directly
membership can change freely, shares of a public company transfer without consent, and the common seal stands in for the signature the law cannot give an artificial person

concepts.title: Kinds of Companies
concepts.definition: Companies divide by how far members must pay (limited by shares, limited by guarantee, or unlimited) and by who may own them: a private company needs at least 2 and at most 200 members, while a public company starts at 7 with no upper cap.
concepts.key_idea: The liability clause answers how much a member can lose; the membership clause answers who is allowed to hold the company.

solution_steps.explain: shares-basis caps risk at the unpaid nominal value, guarantee-basis at the promised amount on winding up, unlimited exposes personal wealth

a public company whose shares trade on a recognised stock exchange is listed; otherwise it is unlisted

concepts.title: Categories of Share Capital
concepts.definition: Share capital appears in nested layers: the Memorandum fixes the authorised amount, the company offers part of it as issued capital, applicants take up part of that as subscribed capital, directors call up part of the subscribed amount, and shareholders actually pay part of the called amount.
concepts.key_idea: Each layer can only be a slice of the one above it, and uncalled capital kept aside solely for winding up is the reserve capital.

solution_steps.action: order the layers from the Memorandum down
solution_steps.explain: authorised (registered) capital heads the list, issued capital is the portion actually offered, subscribed capital is what the public took

solution_steps.action: split the subscribed layer by payment status
solution_steps.explain: called up capital is what the company has demanded so far; paid up capital is what has actually landed; the gap is calls in arrears

solution_steps.explain: the note shows authorised, issued and subscribed amounts, deducts calls in arrears from the called up figure, and carries the rest as a footnote

concepts.title: Paid-up Capital after Calls in Arrears
concepts.definition: Reported paid-up capital equals what was demanded on all subscribed shares minus what defaulting shareholders still owe on the calls already made.
concepts.key_idea: The note to accounts shows the deduction line by line so the reader can see both the demand and the default.
question_patterns: calculate the paid up capital after some shareholders miss a call

solution_steps.action: total the demand on all subscribed shares
solution_steps.explain: multiply the number of subscribed shares by the amount called per share
multiply the defaulting shares by the per-share amount left unpaid on the call
paid up capital is the called up total less the arrears

concepts.title: Preference and Equity Shares
concepts.definition: The Companies Act recognises two classes: preference shares hold a fixed-rate first claim on dividends and first repayment of capital at winding up, while equity (ordinary) shares vote, take the residual profit, and rank behind the preference holders.
concepts.key_idea: Preference means priority in pay-out but usually no vote; equity means the vote and whatever profit survives the preference claim.

solution_steps.explain: fixed-rate dividend before equity, and capital refund before equity on winding up
cumulative or non-cumulative, participating or not, redeemable or not, depending on the terms in the Memorandum and Articles
equity shares are defined as everything that is not a preference share; their dividend floats with leftover profit

concepts.title: Minimum Subscription Rule
concepts.definition: Directors must judge, before allotting, that enough money has been raised to cover property bought, issue expenses, borrowed repayments and working capital; SEBI keeps the floor at ninety percent of the issued amount within the prescribed window, failing which everything received is refunded.
concepts.key_idea: No allotment without the floor; a late refund carries interest from the day after the subscription list closes.

solution_steps.explain: money received must reach at least 90% of the issued amount within 120 days of the prospectus
allotment cannot proceed and the entire application money must go back within the prescribed period
refund delayed beyond the statutory days from list closure carries interest at 15% under the Act

concepts.title: Instalment Schedule and Call Amount Due
concepts.definition: A share's price is collected in stages -- application, allotment, then calls -- and whatever the earlier stages did not collect becomes the per-share amount of the closing call, multiplied by the shares allotted to give the money due on that call.
concepts.key_idea: No single call may cross a quarter of the face value, calls need a month's gap and fourteen days' notice, and the last call is labelled final.
question_patterns: find the amount due on the second and final call of an issue

solution_steps.action: reduce the face value by what earlier stages collected
solution_steps.explain: subtract application, allotment and any earlier call amounts from the face value per share
multiply the per-share balance by the shares allotted to get the amount due on that call

concepts.title: Pro-rata Adjustment of Excess Application Money
concepts.definition: When an issue is oversubscribed and shares are allotted in proportion, the application money beyond what the allotted shares need is kept and squared off against the allotment money due; only the leftover, if any, is refunded or parked as calls in advance.
concepts.key_idea: Rejected applicants get full refunds; pro-rata applicants get their surplus applied against allotment, so the bank receipt on allotment day shrinks by the adjusted amount.
question_patterns: compute the allotment money still to be received after pro-rata adjustment

solution_steps.action: total the application money that arrived
solution_steps.explain: multiply shares applied for by the application money per share

solution_steps.action: isolate the part earned by allotted shares
solution_steps.explain: multiply shares actually allotted by the same per-share application money
the difference is excess application money available for adjustment

solution_steps.action: net the cash to collect on allotment
solution_steps.explain: deduct the adjusted surplus from the allotment demand; the rest is received in cash (or refunded if the surplus outruns the demand)

concepts.title: Calls in Arrears and Interest Thereon
concepts.definition: Money a shareholder fails to pay on the allotment or on a call by the due date sits as calls in arrears; the articles (or Table F by default) let the company charge interest on it, capped at ten percent per annum for the days it stays unpaid.
concepts.key_idea: Arrears reduce paid-up capital in the note; interest is income credited to the interest account when it is actually received.
question_patterns: compute interest on calls in arrears at ten percent per annum

solution_steps.explain: multiply the shares in default by the per-share amount left unpaid
apply the article or Table F rate (not above 10% p.a.) to the arrears for the months outstanding

concepts.title: Calls in Advance
concepts.definition: Money taken from shareholders before the matching call is made is a liability, not capital: it rests in a calls in advance account under current liabilities and is transferred to the call account only when that call actually falls due.
concepts.key_idea: Advance money never counts as paid-up capital; Table F caps the compensating interest at twelve percent per annum from receipt until the call is due.
question_patterns: compute interest payable on calls received in advance

solution_steps.explain: bank is debited and calls in advance credited; the balance sits outside share capital until adjustment

solution_steps.action: carry interest for the waiting period
solution_steps.explain: apply the article or Table F rate (not above 12% p.a.) from receipt to the date the call is due

solution_steps.action: adjust when the call is due
solution_steps.explain: calls in advance is debited and the particular call account credited, converting the liability into called-up capital

concepts.title: Forfeiture of Shares
concepts.definition: For non-payment of allotment or call money the company can cancel a shareholder's shares: it debits share capital with the called-up amount on those shares, credits the unpaid amounts to the arrears or call accounts, and parks whatever was actually received in a share forfeiture account.
concepts.key_idea: Reverse everything except an already-received premium: if premium was never collected, securities premium is debited too at the time of forfeiture.
question_patterns: pass the forfeiture entry for shares on which a call was not paid

solution_steps.action: debit capital with what was called
solution_steps.explain: multiply the forfeited shares by the amount called up per share to get the share capital debit
multiply the same shares by the per-share money that was never paid; this credits the call or arrears accounts (and securities premium if premium went unpaid)

solution_steps.action: credit what the shareholder did pay
solution_steps.explain: called-up minus unpaid is the amount collected on those shares, credited to share forfeiture

concepts.title: Reissue of Forfeited Shares and Capital Reserve
concepts.definition: Forfeited shares may be reissued at par, premium or a discount, but the discount on reissue can never outstrip the amount already collected on those very shares at forfeiture; whatever survives of the forfeiture credit for the reissued shares is a capital profit moved to capital reserve.
concepts.key_idea: Only the slice of forfeiture credit belonging to reissued shares reaches capital reserve; the credit for shares still unreissued stays in the forfeiture account.
question_patterns: compute the capital reserve on reissue of forfeited shares

solution_steps.action: take the forfeiture credit for the shares being reissued
solution_steps.explain: multiply the reissued shares by the amount that had been received on each at forfeiture
multiply the reissued shares by face value minus reissue price; it may not exceed the forfeited amount
forfeited amount on the reissued shares less the discount is the capital gain, transferred to capital reserve
